faq.q: Why is frame time more informative than average FPS?
faq.a: Average FPS obscures brief, severe pauses. If a game renders 59 frames in 500 milliseconds and spends 500 milliseconds stuck on a single frame, the average frame rate still appears as 60 FPS, even though the user experiences a jarring half-second freeze. Frame time graphs reveal the exact duration of each rendered frame.

faq.q: What do 1% Low and 0.1% Low metrics mean?
faq.a: The 1% Low represents the 99th percentile slowest frame times in a benchmark dataset, converted to an equivalent frame rate. The 0.1% Low captures the single worst 0.1% of stutter frames (the 99.9th percentile). When 1% lows diverge substantially from the average FPS, perceptible stuttering and pacing instability are present.

faq.q: What is the frame budget for a 60 FPS game?
faq.a: At 60 FPS, the GPU and CPU pipeline must render and present each frame in exactly 16.67 milliseconds (1,000ms / 60). At 120 FPS, the budget shrinks to 8.33 milliseconds.

faq.q: What causes uneven frame pacing on consoles or PCs?
faq.a: Uneven frame pacing occurs when frames are rendered at alternating durations (such as 16.6ms followed by 33.3ms), or when the game's internal frame limiter does not align with the display's vertical refresh interval. Proper frame-rate caps or Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) stabilize delivery intervals.

articleHtml:
Frame Pacing, Frame Budgets, and Percentile Metrics

High average frame rates can deceive human perception when individual frames are delivered at erratic temporal intervals. Consistent frame pacing—ensuring each rendered frame persists on screen for an identical millisecond duration—is the foundational prerequisite for visual smoothness.

The Reciprocal Relationship Between FPS and Frame Time

Frame rate expresses the quantity of images presented over an entire second, whereas frame time measures the exact millisecond lifespan of an individual frame:

$$\text{Frame Time (ms)} = \frac{1000}{\text{FPS}}, \quad \text{FPS} = \frac{1000}{\text{Frame Time (ms)}}$$

Under a 60 Hz target, every frame possesses a strict delivery budget of 16.67 milliseconds. If a frame completes rendering in 17.0 milliseconds on a standard fixed-refresh display without VRR, it misses the vertical blanking interval (VBLANK), forcing the display to duplicate the previous frame and creating a noticeable stutter.

Understanding 1% Low and 0.1% Low Percentiles

Modern performance benchmarking evaluates frame delivery across percentile curves rather than arithmetic averages:

  • Mean Frame Rate: Represents overall throughput but fails to capture localized spikes or frame drops.
  • 1% Low FPS (99th Percentile Frame Time): Converts the slowest 1% of frames into an equivalent frame rate. A wide disparity between average FPS and 1% Low (e.g. 60 FPS average with a 28 FPS 1% Low) indicates hitching caused by asset streaming or shader compilation.
  • 0.1% Low FPS (99.9th Percentile Frame Time): Quantifies worst-case momentary freeze events, isolating severe engine hiccups.
